title: Marguerite and the Postcards
premise: After his mother Marguerite's funeral, Coral Crane finds a box of forty-one unsent postcards hidden behind her wardrobe, all addressed to a man named Elias Vane in the coastal town of Saltmere, where Coral was born and from which they fled when he was nine. Reading them, he realizes the postcards chronicle a love his mother abandoned for duty—to the Crane inheritance, to propriety, and to keeping Coral's paternity unspoken. Returning to Saltmere with the letters, Coral discovers Elias is dying and that the town has long protected its own version of the story. In confronting what his mother chose not to send—and choosing at last to say it aloud—Coral claims both his inheritance and his name, ending with Elias's deathbed recognition and Coral mailing the final postcard in his own hand.
about_author: Hazel Underhill is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloging other people's unfinished correspondence before turning to fiction. She writes about inheritances of every kind—the ones we receive, and the ones we refuse.

chapters.title: The Inventory
chapters.summary: Coral, POV, catalogs his mother's house after the funeral, itemizing a life that yields no intimacy—only order. The emotional beat is grief displaced into method; he mourns more easily as an appraiser than a son.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Moving the wardrobe to sell the house, Coral finds a loose panel and a shoebox: forty-one postcards, stamped, addressed, never sent. POV Coral. The beat is vertigo—the discovery that silence had a physical archive all along.

chapters.title: Postcard One
chapters.summary: Coral reads the earliest card, dated two years before his birth, playful and unmistakably in love. Intercut fragments of Marguerite's voice. The beat is seduction by proxy; Coral falls into a mother he never knew.

chapters.title: Saltmere
chapters.summary: Coral drives to the coastal town he left at nine, checking into a guesthouse under a false surname. POV Coral. The beat is dread braided with longing—the place remembers him even if he doesn't remember it.

chapters.title: The House on Tern Street
chapters.summary: Coral locates Elias Vane's address and learns from a neighbor that Elias is ill, cared for by a grandniece, Nell. POV Coral. The beat is cowardice surfacing—he circles the door twice and leaves.

chapters.title: What the Town Keeps
chapters.summary: In the pub, Coral hears the local legend: Marguerite Crane, the heiress who ran off with the lighthouse keeper's son and was fetched home. POV Coral. The beat is the shock of being a character in someone else's story.

chapters.title: Nell
chapters.summary: Nell Vane confronts Coral at the guesthouse, recognizing the family resemblance instantly. POV Nell, wary and sharp. The beat is collision—two keepers of the same secret meeting across a breakfast table.

chapters.title: Postcards Nine Through Twenty
chapters.summary: Reading by lamplight, Coral traces the courtship deepening—and the first card that mentions 'the arrangement' with the Crane estate. POV Coral. The beat is dawning horror: love was being traded against duty in real time.

chapters.title: The Uncle's Terms
chapters.summary: A flashback chapter, Marguerite's POV circa thirty years past: her uncle offers her the inheritance contingent on ending the affair and never naming the child's father. The beat is the machinery of power closing quietly around a young woman.

chapters.title: The Unsent Middle Years
chapters.summary: Cards written annually on one date—each year a report of Coral's life sent to no one. POV Coral reading. The beat is heartbreak: his mother loved him most in the act of almost telling.

chapters.title: Elias Refuses
chapters.summary: Coral finally knocks; through Nell, Elias declines to see him. POV Coral. The beat is rejection that mirrors his mother's—Coral learns how it feels to be the letter left unanswered.

chapters.title: The Solicitor's File
chapters.summary: Coral visits the family solicitor and discovers the trust terms: the inheritance passes only if the Crane line remains 'uncomplicated.' POV Coral. The beat is rage at a dead man's clauses still governing the living.

chapters.title: Nell's Version
chapters.summary: Nell tells Coral what Elias said about Marguerite over the years—that he waited three winters, then stopped waiting but never left. POV Nell. The beat is compassion complicating grievance; everyone kept something.

chapters.title: Postcard Forty-One
chapters.summary: The final card, written days before Marguerite's death, says only: 'I am ready now. Forgive me the delay.' POV Coral. The beat is devastation—she chose to speak at the exact moment speech became impossible.

chapters.title: The Lighthouse Walk
chapters.summary: Coral walks the cliff path where his parents met, storm coming in, and nearly turns back toward the safe life. POV Coral. The beat is the novel's hinge—almost saying it, one last time, or crossing over.

chapters.title: The Offer Reversed
chapters.summary: Coral meets the trust's trustees and formally contests the inheritance, surrendering the money unless the conditions are struck. POV Coral. The beat is defiance—refusing the corruption his mother was forced to accept.

chapters.title: Elias Opens the Door
chapters.summary: Hearing of the contest, Elias asks to see Coral. Their first conversation is halting, furious, tender. POV alternating. The beat is recognition without absolution—two strangers bound by a woman's silence.

chapters.title: What Marguerite Wanted
chapters.summary: Elias reveals a forty-second postcard Marguerite did send, decades ago, unsigned—which he always knew. POV Elias. The beat is revelation reframing everything: she wasn't silent; she was split.

chapters.title: The Trustees' Countermove
chapters.summary: The trustees threaten litigation and public exposure of the affair to discredit Coral's claim. POV Coral. The beat is rising menace—power defending itself with the very shame it created.

chapters.title: Saying It
chapters.summary: At a town meeting called over the estate dispute, Coral stands and names Elias Vane as his father, publicly, irrevocably. POV Coral. The beat is climax—the twenty-year art of almost ends in a single spoken sentence.

chapters.title: Last Light
chapters.summary: Elias dies at dawn with Coral and Nell at his side, having signed a simple affidavit acknowledging paternity. POV Nell. The beat is grief made clean—no more archives, no more panels behind wardrobes.

chapters.title: The Postcard in His Own Hand
chapters.summary: Coral mails the forty-one cards to the Saltmere lighthouse museum for display, then writes postcard forty-two: 'My name is Coral Vane Crane. I am ready now.' POV Coral. The beat is resolution—inheriting not the money but the voice.
